# A Brief History of Lighthouses

For as long as people have sailed, they have needed guidance home. The earliest navigational lights were simple bonfires lit on hilltops, later raised onto platforms to extend their reach. From these modest beginnings grew one of humanity's most enduring architectural traditions.

The most famous ancient lighthouse was the Pharos of Alexandria, completed around 280 BCE under Ptolemy II. Rising more than 100 meters, it was among the tallest structures in the world and one of the Seven Wonders. A fire burned at its summit, reportedly amplified by polished metal mirrors. It stood for some 1,500 years before earthquakes toppled it, and its name survives in the word for lighthouse in several languages, including the French *phare* and Spanish *faro*. The Romans carried the practice across their empire, building towers at Ostia, Dover, and La Coruña, where the Tower of Hercules still operates today.

After Rome's decline, lighthouse construction dwindled. Medieval lights were often maintained by monks or local guilds, burning wood, coal, or candles. Revival came with expanding maritime trade. France's Cordouan lighthouse, finished in 1611, combined a working beacon with royal apartments and a chapel.

The eighteenth century brought engineering breakthroughs, most dramatically at the Eddystone Rocks off Plymouth. Henry Winstanley's first tower there was swept away in the Great Storm of 1703, taking its designer with it; its successor burned. John Smeaton's third tower, completed in 1759, used interlocking granite blocks, hydraulic lime that set underwater, and a curved profile modeled on an oak tree. It became the template for wave-swept lighthouses worldwide. The Stevenson family of Scotland later extended these methods to perilous sites such as Bell Rock and Skerryvore.

Illumination improved alongside structure. Aimé Argand's hollow-wick oil lamp of the 1780s produced a steady, bright flame, and in 1822 Augustin-Jean Fresnel introduced his revolutionary lens. Using concentric prisms to gather and focus light into a powerful beam, the Fresnel lens allowed a lamp to be seen more than twenty miles away. Fuels progressed from whale oil to colza oil, kerosene, gas, and eventually electricity.

The twentieth century transformed the keeper's solitary profession. Automation, beginning with Gustaf Dalén's sun valve and accelerating after mid-century, gradually removed resident keepers; most lights were unmanned by the 1990s. Radar, radio beacons, and satellite navigation have since reduced mariners' reliance on visual aids.

Yet lighthouses endure. Many still operate as backups to electronic systems, while others have become museums, inns, and cherished landmarks, symbols of vigilance, safety, and the long human struggle with the sea.
